summary: This informational document captures requirements for session peering of voice, presence, instant messaging and other multimedia traffic. It links use cases to protocol solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone companies connect to each other's networks. This lists what the connecting rules should be able to do.

subtitle: What protocols must do so that SIP service providers can exchange voice, video, presence and messaging with each other.

tldr.problem: SIP service providers need to exchange multimedia traffic across their boundaries, but there was no agreed list of what protocols must provide to find peers' border elements and routing data and to secure the exchange.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyses the peering use cases and extracts 17 numbered requirements covering border elements, session establishment data, presence and instant messaging, and security. It names possible solutions without mandating any.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational requirements document. It mandates no protocol and leaves the mandatory-to-implement security mechanisms to future solutions.

today: RFC 6271 is an Informational document, published in June 2011. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Session Peering Is
sections.content:
Peering at the session level is an agreement between parties to exchange multimedia traffic. The document assumes the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is used to set up sessions between SIP Service Providers (SSPs), who are called peers. Peering can be direct, established between two SSPs, or indirect, via a session intermediary that has a trust relationship with the SSPs.

The focus is the boundary of Layer 5 SIP networks: signaling path border elements (SBEs) and the protocol requirements for looking up and routing on session establishment data. SIP user agents, provisioning, media codecs, quality of service, IP connectivity and accounting or capacity control are out of scope. The requirements are meant to be independent of the media type. The document does not mandate any protocol other than SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: Two phone companies agree to pass calls and chat messages to each other. This document is a checklist of what the connection rules need to cover, not the rules themselves.

sections.title: Border Elements (Requirements 1 to 6)
sections.content:
An SSP must be able to declare or advertise the entities that face a peer's network. Requirement 1 says protocol mechanisms MUST let an SSP communicate its ingress SBEs, and Requirement 2 does the same for egress SBEs, which help with capacity planning, traffic engineering and call admission control. Requirement 3 covers the data path border elements (DBEs) that carry media.

Requirement 4 says advertisement of SBEs and DBEs MUST allow peer variability, since an SSP may expose different border elements to different peers. Plain DNS per RFC 3263 is described as under-specified for this, because SIP URIs get passed around by users. The text mentions DNS answers that vary by asker and anycast as possible directions needing further analysis.

Requirement 5 says the Look-Up Function (LUF) and Location Routing Function (LRF) MUST be able to return both a target URI and a value giving the next SIP hop. Requirement 6 says the mechanism for locating a peer's SBE MUST be able to convey how the peer should start secure session establishment, for example SIP over TLS or the SIPS URI scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: Each company has front doors for calls and for sound. The requirements say a company must be able to tell its partners which doors to use, and sometimes give different partners different doors.

sections.title: Session Establishment Data and URIs (Requirements 7 to 9)
sections.content:
Session Establishment Data (SED) is the data used to route a call to the next hop at the called domain's ingress point. SED should rely on URIs, and SIP URIs should be preferred over tel URIs for VoIP peering. Requirement 7 says protocols MUST accommodate different URI types, URIs with the same domain part SHOULD share peering policies, and the host part SHOULD be a fully qualified domain name rather than a numeric address.

Requirement 8 says peering should not require an SSP to know which individual users are valid in a peer's domain. Requirement 9 says mechanisms MUST let an SBE locate its peer SBE given a URI type and the target SSP domain name. The text adds that peering should add minimal overhead and delay, and use caching to avoid extra round trips. Solutions should not rely solely on PSTN identifiers or E.164 numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Calls are addressed by a name like a web address. A company should be able to look up where to send a call from the part after the at sign, without knowing everyone who lives there.

sections.title: Presence and Instant Messaging (Requirements 10 to 14)
sections.content:
Two SSPs may peer so that their presence and instant messaging users can work with each other. The requirements build on use cases from RFC 5344.

  • 10: presence exchange SHOULD allow subscriptions to a single presentity or to personal, public or ad hoc lists.
  • 11: IM exchange SHOULD support methods such as one-time messages, session-based messaging and n-way chat rooms, though SSPs may restrict methods by policy.
  • 12: mechanisms SHOULD allow sharing of per-presentity watcher privacy settings, which cuts duplicate notifications, only with the user's express consent.
  • 13: an SSP SHOULD be able to attach a presence document to a list of watchers in the peer community.
  • 14: systems SHOULD use standard PIDF documents and translate non-standard values to standard ones, so meaning is preserved (for example, Do Not Disturb versus Busy).
sections.plainLanguage: Friends on two different chat apps should still be able to see whether each other is online and send messages, and the apps should agree on what words like 'busy' mean.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Three flows are considered: fetching SED via the LUF and LRF, the SIP signaling between SSPs, and the media. The RFC does not specify mandatory-to-implement security mechanisms, leaving that to future protocol solutions.

Requirements 15 and 16 say protocols for querying the LUF and LRF SHOULD support mutual authentication, and SHOULD provide data confidentiality and integrity, because responses may depend on the requester and carry sensitive routing data. Mutual authentication also helps resist denial-of-service via bogus lookups.

For SIP signaling, the RFC describes desirable properties without new normative requirements, pointing to TLS transport (RFC 3261, RFC 5923) and SIP Identity (RFC 4474). For media, Requirement 17 says peering protocols MUST NOT interfere with media security attributes in SDP, and attribute lines an SBE does not understand MUST be ignored and passed along untouched. Secure RTP (RFC 3711) is given as an example of media protection.
sections.plainLanguage: The lookups should check who is asking, and messages should be sealed. Middlemen must not fiddle with the secret-sound settings that the two callers agree on.
